Harriet Tubman: The Moses of the Eastern Shore. How Araminta Ross escaped from slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland, and returned nineteen times into the slaveholders' stronghold to lead seventy family members and friends to freedom on the Underground Railroad. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into the life of America's greatest liberator.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the dense tidal marshes and pine woods of Dorchester County on Maryland's Eastern Shore, an enslaved young woman named Araminta Ross grew up under the brutal weight of the chattel lash. Suffering a catastrophic traumatic brain injury when an overseer hurled a two-pound iron weight at another slave, she experienced vivid visionary dreams that she believed were direct communications from God. In 1849, facing the auction block, she fled north to Philadelphia, declaring: 'I had reasoned this out in my mind, there was one of two things I had a right to, liberty or death; if I could not have one, I would have the other.' But freedom alone was not enough. Over the next decade, Harriet Tubman returned nineteen times into the lion's den of the slave South, guiding over seventy family members and friends along the Underground Railroad to freedom. She never lost a passenger, and she never ran her train off the track. George brings us the immortal story of Harriet Tubman.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE SALT MARSHES OF DORCHESTER COUNTY
Born into slavery around eighteen twenty-two in Dorchester County on Maryland's Eastern Shore, Araminta Ross—known affectionately as Minty—grew up in a world defined by the brackish tidal rivers and dense pine forests of the Chesapeake basin. From early childhood, Minty was subjected to cruel physical labor, hired out to harsh masters who whipped her for minor infractions and forced her to check muskrat traps in freezing winter marshes. When she was barely twelve years old, an event occurred that permanently altered her life: while visiting a village dry goods store, an enraged overseer threw a heavy two-pound iron merchant weight at an escaping field hand. The iron weight missed its target and struck young Minty directly in the forehead, crushing her skull. For months, she hovered between life and death on a straw pallet. The injury left her with permanent narcolepsy, causing her to fall into sudden, deep trances without warning, as well as intense, vivid spiritual visions that she interpreted as divine guidance from God, instilling in her an unshakeable faith and fearless conviction that the Lord walked beside her in the dark. Minty childhood on the Eastern Shore was shaped by the sound of whip cracks and the constant fear of the Georgia slave traders who arrived in Cambridge to purchase enslaved families for Deep South cotton plantations. The traumatic head wound left Harriet with permanent neurological damage, but she viewed her vivid visionary trances as divine revelations, believing that God voice commanded her to lead her people out of bondage. From early childhood, Araminta worked alongside field hands and timber cutters in the marshlands, developing extraordinary stamina and courage.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE FLIGHT TO PHILADELPHIA AND THE TASTE OF FREEDOM
In eighteen forty-four, Minty married John Tubman, a free Black man, and adopted her mother's first name, becoming Harriet Tubman. But marriage could not shield her from the terror of the domestic slave trade. In the autumn of eighteen forty-nine, following the death of her owner Edward Brodess, Harriet learned that she and two of her brothers were to be sold to chain gangs in the Deep South. On a crisp autumn evening, Harriet slipped into the woods alone, following the North Star along the Choptank River. Guided by Quaker abolitionists and free Black conductors who gave her directions to safe houses, Harriet traveled ninety miles on foot through Maryland and Delaware, navigating swamps by night and sleeping in haystacks by day. Crossing the Pennsylvania state line into Philadelphia, the morning sun illuminated her face. Harriet later recalled the transcendent moment of liberation: 'I looked at my hands to see if I was the same person. There was such a glory over everything; the sun came like gold through the trees, and over the fields, and I felt like I was in heaven.' But she immediately felt an agonizing loneliness: she was free, but her parents, brothers, sisters, and friends remained in chains. Harriet walked along the dark banks of the Choptank River under the autumn moon, her heart pounding with terror as she navigated through pine thickets and waded through icy tidal marshes toward Delaware. Crossing into the free state of Pennsylvania, Harriet felt a wave of transcendent joy, yet the sight of her own free hands only sharpened her burning resolve to return south to rescue her family. Her first steps across the Pennsylvania border filled her with awe, inspiring her lifelong mission to liberate those left behind.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE MOSES OF HER PEOPLE
Refusing to enjoy her liberty while her family suffered in bondage, Harriet took employment as a domestic cook and laundress in Philadelphia, scrimping every penny to finance rescue missions. In December eighteen fifty, she executed her first daring rescue: learning that her niece Kessiah and her two children were to be auctioned on the courthouse steps in Cambridge, Maryland, Harriet infiltrated the town, coordinated with Kessiah's free husband to outbid the slave trader, and spirit the family away to Philadelphia. It was the beginning of an extraordinary decade of clandestine operations. Harriet became the most renowned 'conductor' on the Underground Railroad, earning the awe-inspiring biblical moniker 'Moses.' Operating with supreme tactical discipline, Harriet always scheduled departures on Saturday evenings, knowing that slaveholders could not publish runaway notices in newspapers until Monday morning, buying her groups a crucial thirty-six-hour head start before slave patrols mobilized. In Philadelphia, Harriet was welcomed by legendary Black abolitionist William Still, director of the Philadelphia Vigilance Committee, who recorded the names and harrowing escape stories of every passenger on her underground railroad. Harriet operated with military stealth and unshakeable discipline, using code words, secret knocks, and safe house networks maintained by courageous Quaker families who risked federal imprisonment to assist runaways. Frederick Douglass later remarked that while others spoke from lecture halls, Harriet Tubman repeatedly risked her life in hostile territory.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE TACTICS OF THE MASTER CONDUCTOR
Harriet Tubman's success as an operative was the product of brilliant tactical tradecraft and psychological mastery. She disguised herself as an elderly, stooped beggar woman or an eccentric field hand carrying live chickens, once avoiding capture by letting the chickens loose in a street and chasing them through the dirt while slave catchers walked right past her! She used secret spirituals as code songs: singing 'Go Down Moses' to alert hidden fugitives that danger was near, and 'Steal Away to Jesus' when the coast was clear. In her skirt pockets, she carried paregoric to soothe crying infants so their cries would not betray their hiding places in swamps, and a loaded revolver. The revolver was not only for slave catchers; it was for faint-hearted runaways who grew terrified and wanted to turn back, threatening the entire party. Harriet would point the gun and say calmly: 'You go on or die. Dead folks tell no tales.' Every single passenger she led kept moving forward. Tubman understood the psychology of her pursuers: she knew that slave catchers expected runaways to travel north, so she frequently directed her groups onto southbound trains to throw bounty hunters off their trail. Her loaded revolver was a symbol of absolute operational security: she knew that if a frightened fugitive turned back, torture by slave catchers would force them to reveal the locations of safe houses and conductors. She carried a revolver to encourage frightened passengers who contemplated turning back and risking the capture of the entire group.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: DEFYING THE FUGITIVE SLAVE LAW TO CANADA
In September eighteen fifty, Congress passed the draconian Fugitive Slave Act, making it a federal crime to assist runaways and empowering federal marshals to capture self-liberated people in free Northern states without jury trials. Philadelphia and New York were no longer safe sanctuaries. Harriet adjusted her operations with characteristic audacity: she extended her underground railroad route all the way to St. Catharines in Ontario, Canada, guiding fugitives across the suspension bridge over the roaring gorge of Niagara Falls into British sovereign territory where Queen Victoria's laws guaranteed absolute freedom. As reward posters offering thousands of dollars for her capture were posted across the South, Harriet boldly returned to Maryland again and again. In eighteen fifty-seven, she executed her most perilous mission: rescuing her elderly, frail parents, Benjamin and Rit Ross, who were facing arrest for harboring runaways. Harriet transported them in a modified horse-drawn cart by night to Philadelphia and on to Auburn, New York, where legendary abolitionist Senator William H. Seward sold Harriet a modest farm on generous terms. The passage of the Fugitive Slave Law turned Northern states into a hunting ground for slave catchers, prompting Harriet to extend her underground railroad routes into the British sovereign sanctuary of St. Catharines, Canada. Harriet escorted her elderly parents through winter blizzards in a horse-drawn cart, disguising them under blankets and safely delivering them to a peaceful haven in upstate New York. In St. Catharines, Canada West, Tubman established a welcoming haven where newly liberated Black families found shelter and dignified employment.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE RAID ON THE COMBAHEE FERRY
When the Civil War erupted in eighteen sixty-one, Harriet Tubman offered her extraordinary skills directly to the Union army. Serving in coastal South Carolina as a nurse, scout, and military spy for the Department of the South, Harriet recruited a network of river pilots and scouts who gathered critical intelligence behind Confederate lines. On June second, eighteen sixty-three, Harriet achieved an unprecedented milestone in American military history: under the direction of Union Colonel James Montgomery, Harriet Tubman became the first woman in United States history to plan and lead an armed military assault—the Raid on the Combahee Ferry. Guiding three federal gunboats past submerged Confederate torpedoes and river mines, Harriet's force landed Union troops who burned multimillion-dollar Confederate rice plantations, destroyed bridges, and liberated over seven hundred and fifty enslaved men, women, and children who rushed to the riverbanks singing hymns of jubilee. During the Combahee Ferry raid, Harriet stood on the deck of the Union gunboat singing spirituals to calm the panicked crowds of enslaved families who rushed through Confederate rice fields to reach the federal ships. The Combahee River expedition was a masterpiece of military logistics, liberating over seven hundred people and destroying thousands of dollars in Confederate military supplies without losing a single Union soldier. Her brilliant leadership during the Combahee River expedition earned her the admiration of Union generals as a military scout and commander.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE ETERNAL TORCH OF FREEDOM
Following the Union victory, Harriet Tubman returned to her modest brick home in Auburn, New York, dedicating the remainder of her long life to charitable service. She opened her home to elderly, impoverished freedmen, orphans, and the disabled, establishing the Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged, while actively campaigning alongside Susan B. Anthony for women's suffrage. When she passed away in nineteen thirteen at the extraordinary age of ninety-one, she was buried with full military honors at Fort Hill Cemetery. Harriet Tubman remains an towering colossus of moral courage and self-sacrifice, a five-foot-tall woman born into bondage who never held a day of formal schooling, yet outsmarted an empire of human bondage through sheer intelligence, faith, and unbreakable will. Today, the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Historical Park on the Eastern Shore preserves the tranquil marshes and winding rivers where she walked in the dark, an eternal beacon of freedom that will illuminate the conscience of America for all time. In her later years in Auburn, Harriet continued her tireless work for human dignity, opening a home for aged African Americans and marching alongside Susan B. Anthony to demand voting rights for all women. Harriet Tubman legacy is etched into the bedrock of American history, an immortal reminder that true freedom is earned through selfless sacrifice, fearless determination, and an unwavering commitment to justice. Harriet Tubman's life stands as a towering beacon of moral courage, tactical genius, and selfless sacrifice for human dignity.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Harriet Tubman proved that courage, faith, and selfless devotion could conquer the darkest tyranny on earth. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we mount horses in Delaware for Caesar Rodney's desperate midnight gallop for independence.
